overview: This file documents U.S. occupation authorities’ policies and practical guidance concerning access to telephone and communications services in Japan by foreign commercial firms and other non-occupation users in 1948–1949. Despatch No. 540 and its enclosures distinguish occupation agencies from commercial organizations, direct businesses to Japanese telephone offices, establish service priorities, and explain high installation costs, compulsory government bonds, material shortages, and construction delays. Internal State Department memoranda recommend sharing the information with the Department of Commerce. A later despatch encloses a technical survey of Japan’s government-owned telephone system, principal urban exchanges, equipment suppliers, long-distance infrastructure, and available Japanese-language technical literature.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 540 on communications services for non-occupation users
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the rules, costs, and practical difficulties facing foreign commercial firms seeking telephone service in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that foreign commercial organizations are not occupation agencies and generally must apply directly to local Japanese telephone offices. Foreign traders reportedly receive a favorable priority and can often obtain service within one or two weeks, but must purchase a ¥36,000 government bond and secure SCAP permission because foreign firms are otherwise prohibited from making yen investments. It also records installation, monthly maintenance, and per-call charges and contrasts foreign access with the expensive market in transferable telephone rights faced by Japanese businesses.

subfiles.title: GHQ directive on provision and procurement of communications services
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by J. F. Bradshaw by command of General MacArthur
subfiles.about: Defines which bodies qualify as occupation agencies and how other users must procure communications services.
subfiles.summary: The directive restricts communications supplied on occupation procurement demand to military and civilian occupation bodies, inter-Allied organizations, accredited official missions, and certain news correspondents. Commercial organizations are expressly excluded and must obtain service from the Japanese Ministry or local communications bureaus. It also directs the Eighth Army to arrange priorities for licensed businesses and requires modification of earlier authorizations that conflict with the new policy.

subfiles.title: List of occupation agencies
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Enumerates the military, civilian, inter-Allied, and national missions classified as occupation agencies.
subfiles.summary: The list identifies U.S. armed services, the State Department, the U.S. Maritime Commission, the Japan Oil Storage Company, and the British Commonwealth Occupation Forces as occupying organizations. It also includes the Far Eastern Commission, Allied Council for Japan, international tribunal and prosecution bodies, and official missions from eleven commission member states.

subfiles.title: List of additional agencies retaining occupation telephone service
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Lists nonstandard organizations permitted to retain occupation telephone service already provided to them.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure grants continued use of existing occupation telephone facilities to the Central Motion Picture Exchange, Coca Cola, Pepsi Cola, LARA, the American Red Cross, and accredited news organizations. It also covers the Danish, Belgian, Norwegian, and Italian diplomatic missions.

subfiles.title: Directive on priorities for non-occupation telephone connections
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by J. F. Bradshaw by command of General MacArthur
subfiles.about: Amends the April directive and establishes procedures for licensed foreign entrants and Japanese organizations requesting telephone priority.
subfiles.summary: Licensed entrants are instructed to apply first to the Japanese telephone office in the city where service is wanted, seeking occupation assistance only when local officials reject or cannot promptly satisfy an essential application. Japanese persons and organizations working for the occupation may receive Class A priority only after their need has been scrutinized and certified as essential. The directive describes engineering limits involving wire and poles, possible waits of up to ninety days, monthly bond-purchase windows, and the need to avoid disrupting Japanese construction programs.

subfiles.title: Ministry of Communications telephone-priority table
subfiles.about: Classifies applicants for telephone subscriptions according to their public importance and contribution to postwar rehabilitation.
subfiles.summary: Class A covers government bodies, foreign-government offices, Diet members, political parties, public utilities, transport, communications, medical facilities, and related essential services. Class B contains an extensive catalog of mining, manufacturing, agriculture, construction, fisheries, commerce, finance, education, cultural, labor, and recreational enterprises important to reconstruction. Class C covers remaining or less necessary applicants, while the remarks allow communications officials to adjust classifications according to local conditions, scale, use, and existing service.

subfiles.title: Nippon Times clipping on the cost of installing a telephone
subfiles.about: Explains the compulsory government-bond purchase and licensing conflict confronting foreign firms that want telephones in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The article reports that Japanese and foreign applicants must buy a ¥36,000 fifteen-year government bond before receiving telephone service. For foreign firms, the purchase conflicts with SCAP licenses prohibiting yen investments, so occupation authorities issue special exceptions. The correspondent emphasizes the bond's $133 official value, four-percent interest rate, and likely erosion through inflation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending transmission of Despatch No. 540 to Commerce
subfiles.from: Harry B. Otterman, Acting Chief, Telecommunications Division
subfiles.about: Recommends sending the telephone-service despatch and its enclosures to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Otterman judges that the despatch requires no State Department action but would interest the Department of Commerce because it describes problems confronting American businesspeople in Japan. Since the Telecommunications Division lacks an extra copy, he forwards the available despatch and enclosure sets for possible transmission.

subfiles.title: Memorandum circulating Despatch No. 540 within the Department
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the despatch and asks whether its information should also be supplied to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the despatch concerns difficulties encountered by foreign and American businesspeople seeking office telephone service in Japan. Although no substantive action appears necessary, TD circulates it because the Political Adviser considered the information useful to prospective commercial visitors. A later notation agrees that Commerce should receive it, if necessary on loan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 175 forwarding information on Japanese telephone operations
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a GHQ memorandum describing telephone-service operations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser encloses a General Headquarters memorandum on Japan's telephone system. The covering despatch states that GHQ had sent the material on March 12, 1949, to the U.S. Army's Civil Affairs Division in Washington for transmission to an American concern that had requested the information. Departmental routing marks assign the matter to the Telecommunications Division.

subfiles.title: Telephone Service Operations in Japan
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: An unidentified American concern, via the U.S. Army Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.about: Provides a technical and commercial overview of Japan's government-owned telephone network, major exchanges, suppliers, and reference literature.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the Japanese Ministry of Communications exclusively owns and operates commercial local and long-distance telephone service and that negotiations with foreign firms remain under GHQ control. It lists populations and switching technologies for ten principal urban exchanges, ranging from step-by-step dial systems to manual common-battery equipment. It also names major equipment, wire, and cable suppliers, explains the limited use of radio links, and identifies a large 1944 Japanese-language communications-engineering reference work.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how a mundane business requirement—obtaining a telephone—was shaped by occupation law, scarce infrastructure, Japanese reconstruction priorities, currency controls, and competing foreign and domestic claims. Its combination of formal directives, a detailed Japanese priority schedule, a contemporary press account, internal State Department routing memoranda, and a technical network survey permits historians to compare official policy with commercial experience. The exchange populations, switching technologies, supplier names, charges, material limits, and telephone-bond rules also provide unusually concrete evidence about the condition and administration of Japan's postwar communications system.
